title: Behind Booking.com's AI Evolution: The Unpolished Story
gist: Booking.com Principal Engineer Jabez Eliezer Manuel traces 20 years of the company's data and ML platforms: a small-shard MySQL fleet of ~7,000 instances used effectively as a cache, a painful multi-year Hadoop exit completed in 1.5 years once leadership went all-in on cloud (92% of workflows deleted), a model-serving platform doing 400B predictions/day under 20ms, three unsuccessful-to-partial feature-store attempts, and a ranking service at 100K rps. Booking.com is now building agentic-AI foundations (memory, agent serving, access control) and unifying its ML platforms under a single orchestration layer.

insights.claim: Booking.com subjects every visitor to 1,000+ concurrent experiments and has run more than 150,000 experiments, with a success rate below 25%.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: A sub-25% hit rate at massive scale shows experimentation velocity, not idea quality, is the moat in consumer internet optimization.
insights.quote: most of our experiments fail, our success rate is just less than 25%. The goal isn't to get it right, but it is to learn fast.

insights.claim: Booking.com uses interleaving (team-draft merging of results from multiple ranking models shown to all users) to pre-select ranking models, achieving roughly a 10x speed-up in variant testing versus A/B tests, then confirms the winner with a proper A/B test.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Interleaving lets search/ranking teams iterate models far faster with less traffic, a tactic relevant to any marketplace ranking business.

themes.theme: MySQL at scale on commodity hardware

insights.claim: Booking.com grew from a single MySQL master with four replicas in 2005 to roughly 7,000 MySQL instances, managed via single-writer topologies, intermediate masters to limit cross-datacenter replication, and the Orchestrator replication tool.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Shows open-source relational databases can scale to hyperscale fleets with automation instead of paid proprietary databases.
insights.locator: Experiments needed data, and that's where

insights.claim: Booking.com keeps MySQL databases small (2TB soft limit, 10TB hard limit) so they fit on local fast storage of commodity server blades, achieving point queries under 350 microseconds and effectively using MySQL as a cache with no separate cache layer.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Small-shard design lowers cost (avoiding iSCSI storage), speeds backups and failovers, and reduces need for caching vendors.
insights.quote: We were effectively using MySQL as a cache.
insights.locator: There are a few things that

insights.claim: Booking.com rebuilds its MySQL fleet every 60 days, which means an automated provisioning action occurs roughly every three minutes.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Fleet-wide automation is a prerequisite for operating databases at this scale; signals demand for database automation tooling.

insights.claim: Booking.com chose to contribute upstream to MySQL rather than fork it, and says GTID-based replication exists because Booking.com proposed it.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Large users shaping open-source roadmaps reduces their maintenance burden versus carrying private forks.
insights.locator: It also provided several side benefits.

insights.claim: Booking.com identified Hadoop's limitations in 2018 but only put it into maintenance mode in 2022 and sunset it about three years later, due to hundreds of petabytes of data, about 190,000 Hadoop tables, 7,000+ workflows and hundreds of teams.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Legacy on-prem big-data estates take many years to unwind, a long tail that sustains cloud migration services demand.
insights.locator: 2011, we introduced Hadoop. 2018, we

insights.claim: Booking.com's on-prem Hadoop suffered from shared mono-version environments, no GPU support, cross-datacenter sync headaches, near-max capacity at peaks, noisy neighbors, and above all no data discovery or ownership.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Lack of GPU support in legacy data platforms is a driver pushing enterprises to cloud for ML.
insights.locator: That worked for us in most

insights.claim: A 2018 attempt to move Booking.com to a cloud provider was shelved (attributed to either cost or a strategy shift), and a later pilot of another cloud did not achieve full migration until leadership mandated an all-in move with no plan B in 2023, after which everything migrated within 1.5 years.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Executive commitment, not technology, was the binding constraint on cloud migration; watch for top-down mandates as a migration catalyst.
insights.quote: In 2023, leadership actually made the call, and they said, guys, we're going to do it all in, no plan B.

insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Most legacy data pipelines are dead weight; migration cost estimates based on full inventories overstate real work.

insights.claim: Booking.com's migration playbook was: map every table and dependency into a graph, trim by usage and lineage, prioritize survivors by graph centrality and impact, migrate in batches, and run a unified command center replacing spreadsheets and tribal knowledge.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: A reusable template for large data migrations; supports demand for lineage and data catalog tooling.
insights.locator: If you look back, one key

insights.claim: Booking.com's retrospective advice is to catalog every asset, establish business and technical ownership, build quality gates before sharing data, and track lineage end-to-end.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Data governance and lineage are positioned as preventive must-haves, a tailwind for data governance vendors.

themes.theme: Model serving at 400B predictions per day

insights.claim: Before 2015, Booking.com faked real-time ML predictions by precomputing predictions over all combinations of input features (e.g., device and country) and storing the results as MySQL lookup tables.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Illustrates how early ML was constrained by serving infrastructure, the gap later filled by model-serving platforms.
insights.locator: This is how we faked it.

insights.claim: A 2015 hackathon Scala model-serving service at Booking.com evolved into a platform supporting 12+ model formats across shared, dedicated and batch clusters behind a custom proxy, able to call externally hosted models such as SageMaker.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Large platforms build in-house serving but still integrate hyperscaler ML services like SageMaker, a hybrid pattern.
insights.locator: Over a period of time, this

insights.claim: Two years before the talk, Booking.com's model-serving platform hosted 480+ models and served 400 billion predictions per day at under 20 milliseconds average latency.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Benchmark for classical ML inference scale at a top online travel agency, separate from LLM inference demand.
insights.quote: It has 480-plus models. It can do 400 billion predictions per day. All of those predictions within less than 20 milliseconds on an average.

insights.claim: In 2015 about 80% of Booking.com data scientists' time was spent on data preparation, with feature duplication across teams and training/inference skew as the main pain points.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Data preparation burden justifies spending on feature stores and data tooling.
insights.locator: Second problem that we started solving

insights.claim: Booking.com's second feature-platform attempt used shared user 'timelines' in HDFS and Cassandra with on-the-fly feature computation, but it failed because scientists were unfamiliar with writing features in Java and fetching Cassandra timelines took more than 90 milliseconds.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: On-the-fly feature computation is too slow for latency-sensitive serving; precomputed lookups win.
insights.locator: We had a wrapper, which had

insights.claim: After three attempts, Booking.com settled on a feature store focused only on storage and serving (ingesting precomputed data-lake and real-time Kafka features into an online store with simple lookups), and still runs three systems for precomputed and real-time features with no unified answer.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Even sophisticated ML shops have not solved feature engineering; the feature-store category remains fragmented and open.
insights.quote: It's a multidimensional problem, and we don't have an answer.

insights.claim: Booking.com's attempt around 2016 to replace its handcrafted hotel ranking formula with machine learning failed for about 1.5 years, largely because Spark ran out of memory on the data volume, until approximations allowed an ML model to win an experiment.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Handcrafted heuristics can be hard to beat; ML replacement timelines in production are often longer than expected.

insights.claim: Personalizing Booking.com's ranking required moving scoring out of a 24-shard scatter-gather availability engine into a separate service, multiplying request volume 24x behind the fanout under tight latency budgets.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Personalization imposes large infrastructure multipliers, raising compute costs for marketplaces.
insights.locator: That's what we wanted to do.

insights.claim: As of 2024, Booking.com's ranking service handled 100,000 requests per second with p99.9 latency of 100 milliseconds and averages of 40-50 milliseconds.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Shows the scale of real-time personalized ranking in online travel.
insights.locator: That's what we wanted to do.

insights.claim: Booking.com frames ranking as a three-way optimization between traveler choice and value, partner exposure and growth, and business efficiency and revenue.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Marketplace ranking trade-offs directly affect take rates and partner relations.

insights.claim: Booking.com runs five ML platforms (GenAI, content intelligence, ranking, recommendations with 40-50 use cases, and value intelligence for promotions), with the GenAI platform providing guardrails, evaluation, orchestration and PII masking for trip planning, smart filters, review summaries, property Q&A and booking support.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Online travel agencies are deploying GenAI across the funnel including customer support, which may reduce support costs.
insights.locator: Now in that third layer, we

insights.claim: Since 2025, Booking.com has been building agentic-system foundations including episodic, semantic and procedural memory, agent serving, agent access and delegation controls, and agent-to-agent communication.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Large consumer platforms are investing in agent infrastructure, signaling agentic commerce in travel is a strategic priority.

insights.claim: Booking.com is unifying its ML platforms under a single orchestration layer to pre-empt fragmentation, enable cross-domain customer experiences, and centralize AI governance, security and quality.
insights.speaker: Jabez Eliezer Manuel
insights.so_what: Platform consolidation for agentic AI suggests demand for centralized AI governance tooling.
